data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma dissolves if we treat the preference for corroborated theories as a convention or decision postulate, similar to choosing axioms, rather than a derived logical consequence.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decision itself requires an inductive justification to be considered rational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists cannot coherently maintain a stance that their actions have no expected link to truth.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If this conventionalism undermines the objective status of scientific knowledge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper explicitly frames the choice of the best-tested theory as a 'decision.' In this view, there is no logical bridge between 'survived tests' and 'should be used.' The bridge is built by a voluntary commitment to a rule of procedure: 'We decide to act as if the best-tested theory is the most reliable.' This avoids smuggling in induction because it makes no claim about the world guaranteeing the theory's success; it only establishes a normative rule for the scientific community. The cost is high: it renders the rationality of science entirely internal to the game of science, offering no external guarantee that this game leads to truth or practical success, potentially opening the door to relativism.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
